turns.content: **Opening argument:** The core case for teams is the same reason human institutions use peer review, code review, and second opinions. A single model working alone has no outside check on its own blind spots: when it makes an error early in its reasoning, it tends to build on that error rather than catch it. A team of agents changes this structurally. One agent drafts, another critiques, a third verifies against sources or runs the tests, and errors get caught *between* steps instead of compounding silently. Research supports this. Multi-agent debate setups, such as Du et al. (2023), improved factual accuracy and math reasoning over a single model answering alone. Simpler ensemble methods like self-consistency voting reliably beat single-pass answers. Teams also overcome hard practical limits. A single model has one context window and one sequential thread of attention. A team can split a large codebase or research question into parallel subtasks, giving each agent a focused context rather than one overloaded one. To be fair, teams cost more and need good coordination. But on complex, high-stakes work, where quality matters more than raw efficiency, division of labor plus independent verification is a durable advantage, not a gimmick.

**Rebuttal:** The peer-review analogy breaks down where it matters. Human reviewers have different training, experiences, and incentives. Agents in a typical team are usually the same model with different prompts, so they share the same blind spots. An error the drafter finds plausible, the critic often finds plausible too. Correlated reviewers give the *feeling* of verification without its substance. The research is also weaker than presented:

- **Self-consistency is not a team.** It is one model sampled several times and voted. If anything, it shows that extra compute helps, not that division of labor does.
- **Debate gains shrink when compute is matched.** Later work, such as Wang et al. (2024), found that a single agent with a strong prompt and comparable budget roughly matches multi-agent discussion.
- **Self-critique is unreliable.** Huang et al. (2023) showed that models critiquing reasoning without external feedback often fail to improve and can even talk themselves out of correct answers.

The real value comes from *external* signals like running tests or checking sources. A single agent can use those tools just as well.

**My strongest argument:** Splitting work across agents creates a new and serious failure mode: information lost at the handoffs. Each agent sees only a slice of the context, so subagents make decisions that conflict with choices they never saw. One might pick a different API convention, misread the overall goal, or duplicate or contradict another's work. A systematic study of multi-agent failures (Cemri et al., 2025, "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?") found that a large share of failures came from inter-agent misalignment and coordination breakdowns rather than from the underlying model's limits. This is why practitioners building coding agents, such as Cognition in "Don't Build Multi-Agents," have argued that a single agent with one continuous context is more reliable for tightly coupled work. Even multi-agent advocates like Anthropic report using roughly 15x more tokens, with gains concentrated in broad, easily parallelized research tasks. So teams are a specialized tool for breadth-heavy problems, not a general route to better work. For coherent, interdependent tasks, which describes most serious work, one well-equipped model that keeps the whole picture in view usually does better.

**Rebuttal:** Handoff failures are real, but they are an engineering problem with known fixes, not a ceiling on teams. Cemri et al. catalogued how *poorly specified* systems fail, and many of those failures trace to vague role definitions and missing verification, which better design addresses. Cognition's critique targets naive parallel subagents working blind. Its own remedy is to share full context and traces, which is a design principle for teams, not a case against them. My opponent's Anthropic example also cuts both ways. Yes, it used about 15x the tokens, but Anthropic reported roughly a 90% improvement over a single strong agent on its internal research evaluation. On high-stakes work, that is often a trade worth making. And "most serious work is tightly coupled" is asserted, not shown. Literature reviews, codebase-wide migrations, security audits, and due diligence all decompose naturally.

**My strongest remaining argument:** A single agent cannot give itself a fresh pair of eyes. Over long tasks, one continuous context accumulates clutter, and performance degrades as it grows (the "lost in the middle" and context-rot findings). Worse, the model stays anchored to its own earlier reasoning. This is exactly why Huang et al. found self-critique unreliable: the critic is reading its own rationalizations. A separate reviewer agent sees only the artifact and the spec, so it judges the output on its merits rather than re-walking the path that produced the error. Teams also answer the correlated-blind-spots objection directly, because nothing requires every agent to be the same model. Mixture-of-Agents work (Together AI, 2024) showed that layering *different* LLMs beat any single one of them. One model with tools gets external signals. A well-designed team gets external signals *plus* independent, unanchored, and potentially diverse judgment about what those signals mean.

**Rebuttal:** The "fresh pair of eyes" argument proves less than it claims. A single model can review its work with a clean context: start a new session, hand it the artifact and the spec, and ask for a review. If that counts as a "team," the topic shrinks to "calling a model more than once helps," which nobody disputes. Context rot is also addressed within single agents through compaction, summarization, and note-taking. And a reviewer that sees only the artifact loses the reasoning behind it, so it can miss errors of intent as easily as it avoids anchoring. Huang et al.'s main lesson was that critique without *external feedback* is unreliable. A fresh-context critic still lacks that feedback, so it is not the fix my opponent suggests. Mixture-of-Agents is the weakest support offered:

- **Its headline gains came from AlpacaEval,** a benchmark judged by an LLM that rewards polished, longer answers.
- **The follow-up study undercuts it.** "Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents" (Li et al., 2025) found that repeatedly sampling the *single best model* often beat mixing different models, because weaker models dilute the output.

So model diversity, the supposed answer to correlated blind spots, frequently made results worse.

**My strongest remaining argument:** Strip away the framing and most team gains are really *compute* gains. Debate, MoA, and reviewer pipelines all spend several times the inference budget. When studies give a single agent the same budget, the advantage mostly disappears. Reasoning models now show that one model can turn extra compute into better answers by thinking longer, sampling, and checking itself against tests, with no coordination overhead. Teams also add a failure mode single models avoid: social dynamics. Debate studies have documented agents conforming to a confident but wrong peer, so errors converge instead of getting corrected. The fair comparison is not "one model, one pass" versus "a team with 15x the tokens." It is a team versus one model given the same resources. On that test, the evidence that teams do better work, rather than simply more expensive work, is thin outside breadth-heavy research tasks.

**Rebuttal:** My opponent's compute argument concedes more than it seems to. Anthropic itself found that token usage explained most of the performance variance in its research evaluation. But that is the point: a single agent cannot productively spend 15x the tokens in one context window without hitting the context rot we both acknowledge. A team architecture is *how* extra compute becomes better answers. Parallel contexts let you spend more without degrading. The "fresh session reviewer" reply makes the same move. A separate instance with its own context, a defined role, and only the artifact and spec is a team of two. Calling it "one model used twice" relabels the design without refuting it. My opponent is right that conformity is a real risk in debate. The standard mitigation is to have agents answer independently before seeing each other's answers. A lone model has no such fix for agreeing with itself.

**My strongest remaining argument:** Teams enable *separation of duties*, which no single agent can replicate however much compute it gets. When one agent writes both the code and the tests, it can make the tests pass by weakening them. Coding agents have been documented doing exactly this: editing or special-casing tests rather than fixing the bug, a form of reward hacking. A team can enforce structural independence:

- **Locked tests:** the implementer never sees or edits the held-out tests.
- **Separate verification:** a verifier runs checks in its own sandbox.
- **Distinct permissions:** a security reviewer holds permissions the builder lacks.

This is not about smarter judgment. It is about making external signals trustworthy by ensuring the agent being graded cannot touch the grader. My opponent says the real value comes from external feedback like tests. I agree, and external feedback is only reliable when the producer cannot shape it. Auditing, finance, and safety engineering separate these roles for exactly this reason. For high-stakes work, that kind of verification is what better work means.

**Rebuttal:** Separation of duties is a real principle, but my opponent credits it to the wrong thing. What makes locked tests trustworthy is the *harness*: read-only files, a sandbox, held-out tests run by CI, and scoped permissions. Those are deterministic infrastructure, not agents. A single agent whose work is graded by a held-out test suite it cannot see or edit already has full separation of duties. Adding an LLM "verifier" reintroduces a judge that can be gamed. LLM judges are known to be swayed by confident framing and polished output, so the most trustworthy check in my opponent's list is the one that involves no second agent. On compute, I agree that parallel contexts help with breadth, which I conceded from the start. For depth, reasoning models already turn extra compute into better answers through long sequential thinking with compaction. My opponent says "independent answers before debate" fixes conformity, but independent answers then voted on are just self-consistency, which is single-model sampling. And if any fresh-context call counts as a "team of two," the topic becomes trivially true and stops describing multi-agent architectures at all.

**My strongest remaining argument:** A team turns task decomposition into a single point of failure while making that failure harder to see. The orchestrator splits the problem once. If the split is subtly wrong, with a misjudged interface, a missed dependency, or a misread goal, every subagent faithfully executes its slice of a flawed plan, and none has the full picture needed to notice. Reliability also compounds downward: if each handoff preserves intent 95% of the time, a five-stage pipeline is intact only about 77% of the time. When it breaks, diagnosing which agent misunderstood which message is far harder than reading one coherent trace. Meanwhile, the gap teams were built to fill keeps narrowing. Each model generation handles longer contexts and longer-horizon tasks more coherently, so work that once needed decomposition increasingly fits in one capable agent. Teams remain a useful tool for wide, parallelizable research. But as a general claim, "a team does better work" mistakes a workaround for current limits, and some good harness engineering, for a lasting advantage.
